reading.body:
Precision agriculture has commercial AI deployments, federal adoption data, and a UN benchmarking framework operating at the same time.

The pattern is a layered ecosystem rather than a single vendor. Deere, CNH Industrial's Raven division, and pure plays like Carbon Robotics and Monarch ship vision-guided spraying, driverless tractors, and laser weeding as farm equipment. Bayer's Climate FieldView and Corteva's Granular turn soil, weather, and yield data into planting prescriptions. Planet Labs, Descartes Labs, and EarthDaily supply the satellite imagery those models consume, while AgGateway and AEM set the data and machinery standards that make the feeds interoperable.

What makes this notable for AI is that adoption is measured, not guessed. USDA ERS publishes precision-agriculture adoption series, Census BTOS covers agriculture-adjacent sectors in its AI-use series, FAO benchmarks digital agriculture globally, and AgFunder indexes venture funding. That measurement layer means deployment can be checked against real yield and income impact rather than model demos. The data does not cover compute, power, or building constraints, and it gives no adoption percentages, revenue figures, or energy use.

summary: Precision agriculture - vision-guided spraying, yield prediction, autonomous equipment - is deployed at commercial scale. Who tracks it: federal adoption data, a UN benchmarking framework, a venture index, and standards bodies, layered over the equipment giants and AI pure-plays actually shipping it.

analysis.body:
The only hard adoption number in this material comes from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which puts AI use in agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting (NAICS 11) at 6.2% of firms, measured as the share answering yes to whether the business used AI in the last two weeks. The prior period is suppressed, and the survey first asked the question in September 2023, so there is no trend line to read here, only a level. Everything else in the record is vendor, funder, standards body or international organization material rather than a measured rate of use.

Where the sources describe deployment, it clusters around machines and prescriptions. John Deere's precision agriculture line, which the site's notes describe as including See and Spray and autonomous tractors, is presented as the reference commercial deployment. Carbon Robotics describes itself as the leader in physical AI for agriculture, shipping the LaserWeeder and Carbon Autonomy to reduce costs, eliminate weeds, increase yields and improve farm sustainability, with its Carbon AI powered by a Large Plant Model trained on what it calls the world's largest, most diverse and fastest growing agricultural dataset collected by LaserWeeders. Raven, a brand of CNH, provides automated and autonomous farm technologies and precision ag solutions it says improve productivity, sustainability and profitability, and its machines retain stock tractor controls so an operator can switch between manual and autonomous operation. Bayer's Climate FieldView is the platform layer, turning field data into planting and input prescriptions, and Planet Labs supplies the observation layer through daily satellite imagery and analytics, with agriculture listed among its industries and agricultural monitoring among its applications.

AgFunder, which publishes the sector's investment research, reports global agrifoodtech funding hit $16.2 billion in 2025, almost flat versus the prior year at -3%, with investors writing checks more selectively and directing capital toward companies with tangible science, real unit economics and clear paths to revenue. It also reports global agrifoodtech reaching $16 billion in 2024, a 4% drop from 2023, and funding in developing markets growing 63% between 2023 and 2024 against a 4% decline globally. In Asia-Pacific, startups raised $4.2 billion as of the end of October 2024, a 38% increase on the $3.1 billion raised over the same period in 2023. African agrifoodtech raised $145 million in the first half of 2024, a 1.6% year-over-year increase but still just 1.6% of global investment, after a 2023 in which investment declined 62% to $275 million, and deal counts stayed nearly flat at 129 in 2023 against 133 in 2022, which AgFunder reads as smaller deal sizes.

Concrete return figures are thin and mostly come from vendors. Climate FieldView states that farmers using FieldView seed scripts saw an average increase of +5 bu/ac compared to users who wrote their own scripts, and it describes a dealer-facing tool that combines field data with dealer expertise, plus a FieldView Drive 2.0 that sends seed scripts without a thumb drive, has built-in GPS, faster data syncing and compatibility with a wider range of equipment. Carbon Robotics claims cost reduction, weed elimination, yield increases and improved sustainability, and Raven claims maximizing yield with less resources. The site's notes describe the FAO's digital agriculture program, with a 60 Decibels-supported Digital Agriculture Index, as benchmarking platform adoption and real-world yield and income impact, but the FAO page excerpt itself shows community of practice work and the Global AgriInno Challenge rather than index results.

Underneath the products sits a standards and science layer. AgGateway, a global non-profit, works to promote the industry's transition to digital agriculture and expand the use of information to maximize efficiency and productivity, and its Traceability Initiative in North America covers seeding and provenance including grain traceability, while a European special interest group on farm and crop field identification aims to link crop data from different industry sources through standard identifiers, with stated benefits in product management, customer service, food safety and regulatory compliance. The International Society of Precision Agriculture is the scientific organization connecting remote sensing and spatial analytics research to practice, and it maintains a Precision Agriculture Definition available in over fifteen languages, with the 17th ICPA and 11th ConBAP scheduled for summer 2026. The Association of Equipment Manufacturers brings agricultural OEMs together to shape policy, understand data and develop strategies around environmental, political and economic change, and USDA's Economic Research Service is described in the site's notes as publishing the federal data series on precision agriculture adoption across US farms, covering variable-rate technology, yield monitoring and autonomous equipment. The site's notes also list the World Economic Forum's 100 Million Farmers initiative as tracking AI adoption through climate-smart and regenerative agriculture metrics globally.

Regulatory and risk signals in this material are indirect. AgGateway frames standard identifiers and traceability as contributing to food safety and regulatory compliance, which is the clearest regulatory thread, and AEM frames policy engagement as a response to environmental, political and economic pressure on agriculture. AgFunder's read on selective capital and the demand for real unit economics is the main financial caution, and the FAO material on climate-vulnerable food systems and scarce water, including a 400-square-metre greenhouse shared with five other farmers in Kandahar province, points to resource constraints as a driver rather than a risk to adoption. For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the honest summary is that measured AI use in this sector stands at 6.2% of firms per the Census Bureau, the commercial activity is concentrated in autonomous equipment, computer vision and prescription platforms from a handful of large vendors, the funding environment rewards demonstrable science and unit economics, and the published ROI evidence is largely vendor-reported, with the standards bodies and USDA ERS supplying the measurement and interoperability groundwork that any deployment will depend on.

https://climate.com/.brief: Climate FieldView describes itself as an all-in-one digital farming solution for making data-driven decisions, with a separate version built for dealers that combines field data with their expertise. The page states that farmers using FieldView seed scripts saw an average increase of +5 bu/ac compared with users who wrote their own scripts. It also describes FieldView Drive 2.0, which it says can send seed scripts without a thumb drive, has built-in GPS, syncs data faster and works with a wider range of equipment. Other parts of the page point to farmer case studies, support for field trials, and planning checklists.

https://www.aem.org/.brief: AEM describes itself as an association that advances construction and agriculture equipment manufacturers in the global marketplace, and says it works across four areas: advocacy, safety, trade shows and events, and market data. It says it owns and organizes events that connect members with customers worldwide, and that its advocacy work covers grassroots campaigns, public affairs and research. AEM states it is holding a Momentum event in 2026 in Gainesville, GA, intended to deepen connections and deliver industry insights. It also says thousands of industry peers subscribe to its Industry Advisor publication for updates about equipment manufacturing.

https://www.ispag.org/.brief: The International Society of Precision Agriculture is a scientific organization that develops technologies to help feed the world and improve quality of life. It offers a definition of precision agriculture in more than fifteen languages and gives members access to directories, networking, and discounted conference registration. Members receive a monthly “ISPA newsletter” that shares news, job listings, and event information, and the society is preparing for the 17th ICPA and 11th ConBAP in summer 2026. Country Representatives promote ISPA worldwide; applicants must email info@ispag.org with a bio, CV, and be current members, and members can post job announcements on the site and in newsletters.

https://www.planet.com/.brief: Planet Labs offers a platform called Planet Insights that brings together daily satellite imagery, derived data products, and cloud-based tools in one place. The company claims its imagery is the highest-frequency commercial Earth observation data, enabling daily monitoring, high-resolution tasking, and deeper derived insights. It says the platform lets users view the planet in time, space, and frequency, helping them make decisions quickly and confidently. Planet reports that organizations across many sectors use the platform to address operational challenges with a global, dynamic perspective.

https://www.ers.usda.gov/.brief: ERS's State Fact Sheets, the service says, cover population, income, poverty, food security, education, employment, farm characteristics, farm financial indicators, top commodities and agricultural exports, with data for all states and for metro and nonmetro breakouts within states, plus Puerto Rico where applicable, and links to county-level data where available. The Food Price Outlook, according to ERS, provides food price data and forecasts changes in the Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index for food. ERS also offers Vegetables and Pulses Data, a collection giving statistics on fresh and processed vegetables and dry pulses in the United States, along with some global data for those sectors.

https://agfunder.com/research/.brief: AgFunder reports that global agrifoodtech funding reached $16.2 billion in 2025, down 3% year-over-year, with investors becoming more selective and favoring companies demonstrating "tangible science, real unit economics, and clear paths to revenue." While overall funding remained relatively flat, regional patterns diverged significantly: developing markets agrifoodtech grew 63% between 2023 and 2024, Asia-Pacific startups raised $4.2 billion as of October 2024 (a 38% increase), and African agrifoodtech showed mild recovery with $145 million raised in the first half of 2024 after a 62% decline in 2023. These trends suggest a sector undergoing consolidation, with capital concentrating in regions and companies meeting stricter investment criteria.

https://www.fao.org/digital-agriculture/.brief: The page presents e-Agriculture as a worldwide community for dialogue and information sharing about information and communication technologies in sustainable agriculture and rural development. It says the initiative grew out of the World Summit on the Information Society’s Action Line C7, and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations was assigned to facilitate it. The page also reports that the Global AgriInno Challenge 2026 chose 13 youth-led solutions from 137 valid applications to take part in a final pitch event in China. It notes that three winners were announced at the final pitch in Hangzhou on 10 September 2026, including AgriKonnekt from Kenya and Berikanpreneur from Indonesia.
